question.:question/problem:
Find $(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2 t^{2} \\ t + 2\end{bmatrix} \\ g(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}t \\ t - 1 \\ - 3 t^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cross product rule, preserving the factor order:

$$
(f\times g)^{\prime}(t)=f^{\prime}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times g^{\prime}(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(-3)=0 \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t^{2})=4 t \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t + 2)=1 \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4 t \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ g^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t)=1 \\ g^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t - 1)=1 \\ g^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(- 3 t^{2})=- 6 t \\ g^{\prime}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ - 6 t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 4 t & 1 \\ t & t - 1 & - 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{1,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}4 t & 1 \\ t - 1 & - 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=- 12 t^{3} - t + 1 \\ P_{1,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ t & - 3 t^{2}\end{vmatrix}=t \\ P_{1,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 t \\ t & t - 1\end{vmatrix}=- 4 t^{2} \\ P_1 & =\begin{bmatrix}- 12 t^{3} - t + 1 \\ t \\ - 4 t^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ P_2 & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -3 & 2 t^{2} & t + 2 \\ 1 & 1 & - 6 t\end{vmatrix} \\ P_{2,1} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 t^{2} & t + 2 \\ 1 & - 6 t\end{vmatrix}=- 12 t^{3} - t - 2 \\ P_{2,2} & =-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & t + 2 \\ 1 & - 6 t\end{vmatrix}=2 - 17 t \\ P_{2,3} & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 2 t^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}=- 2 t^{2} - 3 \\ P_2 & =\begin{bmatrix}- 12 t^{3} - t - 2 \\ 2 - 17 t \\ - 2 t^{2} - 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\times g)^{\prime}(t) & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}- 24 t^{3} - 2 t - 1 \\ 2 - 16 t \\ - 6 t^{2} - 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}$ given that $f(t)=⟨e^{- t},\,e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩$ and $v(t)=e^{t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar function multiple rule:

$$
(v(t)f(t))^{\prime}=v(t)f^{\prime}(t)+v^{\prime}(t)f(t)
$$

Differentiate each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}_{1}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{- t})=- e^{- t} \\ f^{\prime}_{2}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{3 t})=3 e^{3 t} \\ f^{\prime}_{3}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{t + 3})=e^{t + 3} \\ f^{\prime}(t) & =⟨- e^{- t},\,3 e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩ \\ v^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(e^{t})=e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the first product-rule term and the second product-rule term, denoted $P_1$ and $P_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P_1 & =(e^{t})⟨- e^{- t},\,3 e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3 e^{4 t},\,e^{t} e^{t + 3}⟩ \\ P_2 & =(e^{t})⟨e^{- t},\,e^{3 t},\,e^{t + 3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,e^{4 t},\,e^{t} e^{t + 3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Add the two terms componentwise:

$$
\begin{aligned}(v(t)f(t))^{\prime} & =P_1+P_2 \\  & =⟨0,\,4 e^{4 t},\,2 e^{2 t + 3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le \pi }
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $r(u,v)=⟨2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u⟩$ for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le \pi .$ What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡v & 1 \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡v & 1 \\ -3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 1 \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v & 0\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡v \\ 2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-6u{sin}^{2}⁡v-6u{cos}^{2}⁡v⟩ \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-6u⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-6u⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)^{2}+(2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)^{2}+(-6u)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v+4{u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(5{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v+4{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v)+4{u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v+4{u}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v)+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v+4{u}^{2}+36{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v+40{u}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡v+8)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{u}^{2}}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡v+8} \\  & =\sqrt{5}u\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡v+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{{u}^{2}}=u$ since $u\ge 0$ on $D.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{5}u\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡v+8}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the surface area of the parametric surface defined by the equations 

$$
x=2u-v,\,y=3u+2,\,z=u+2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $-1\le v\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u-v,\,3u+2,\,u+2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,3,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\,-5,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨6,\,-5,\,3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's denote

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1}.
$$

Then, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{70}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{∬}_{D}\text{ }\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the surface area of the part of the parametric surface $r(u,v)=⟨-u+v,\,u-2v,\,3v⟩$ that is subject to the constraint ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 4.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,3,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨3,\,3,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that the region ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 4$ corresponds to the disk

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\le 4},
$$

of radius $2.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{19}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{19}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{19}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{19}\cdot (\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi \sqrt{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

and 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v & 2{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2v & 2{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2{v}^{2}\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2{v}^{2},\,2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-2{v}^{2},\,2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-2{v}^{2})^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{4}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}({v}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2v\sqrt{{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}

For a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$, the fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Differentiate with respect to one parameter while holding the other fixed.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,2u,\,v\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,1,\,u\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 2u & v \\ 1 & 1 & u\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Each component subtracts two nonzero products. In particular, the middle cofactor has a minus sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_1&=(2u)u-v\cdot1=2u^2-v,\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_2&=-(1\cdot u-v\cdot1)=v-u,\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_3&=1\cdot1-(2u)1=1-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\langle 2u^2-v,\,v-u,\,1-2u\rangle.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u+v,\,uv,\,u\sin(uv)\rangle.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:

The third coordinate requires the product rule when differentiating with respect to $u$, and the chain rule for $\sin(uv)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\bigl(u\sin(uv)\bigr)&=\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv),\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\bigl(u\sin(uv)\bigr)&=u^2\cos(uv).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,v,\,\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv)\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,u,\,u^2\cos(uv)\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & v & \sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv) \\ 1 & u & u^2\cos(uv)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand and simplify one component at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_1&=u^2v\cos(uv)-u\bigl(\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv)\bigr)\\&=-u\sin(uv),\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_2&=-\bigl(u^2\cos(uv)-\sin(uv)-uv\cos(uv)\bigr)\\&=\sin(uv)+u(v-u)\cos(uv),\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_3&=1\cdot u-v\cdot1=u-v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\langle -u\sin(uv),\,\sin(uv)+u(v-u)\cos(uv),\,u-v\rangle.
$$

The first component retains the product-rule term after the two $u^2v\cos(uv)$ terms cancel.
